title: Keep Nil
passages:
Sol handed the wheel to Dey without looking back. "Hold her off the pier," she said. "Don't let her drift into the channel while I'm gone."

Dey was still wet from hauling Nia up the service trunk, his hair plastered to his forehead, one hand wrapped in a rag from the salt burns. "You want me to steer this tub with a surge coming and your credit in the gutter?" he said. "Fine. But if we swing into the gate, I'm telling Quill you ordered it."

"She can't stop a boat with words," Sol said. She tucked the Marrow's bond into the oilskin pouch at her belt and turned for the steel stair.

The Kettle's low gate was a rib of rusted iron sunk into the drowned coast, its lock teeth half-lifted against the incoming tide. Storm season had the water chopping at the pilings, and the arcology loomed behind it like a tooth that hadn't fallen out yet. Sol's boots rang on the stair, each step pulling her higher above the waterline where the good seats were. The bond felt thin against her hip, paper and wax, the Marrow's surety written out to Pru Quill's berth book. Enough to buy six berths, if the count wasn't full. If the warden would open the shutter.

At the top, the dock-warden's box hung over the channel like a crow's nest built by accountants. Glass windows, steel frame, a single lantern burning inside. Sol climbed the last rung and planted her palms on the sill.

The shutter was down.

She knocked once, hard. "Quill. Open up."

No answer. Through the glass she could see the berth book lying on the counter, thick and leather-bound, a heavy chain run through its cover and looped around a bolt in the frame. A second chain locked the shutter itself, padlocked at the hasp. The little window in the door was open just a crack, barely wide enough for a voice, and a slip of paper had been wedged in it.

COUNT FULL, the slip said in Quill's sharp hand. NO BERTHS BEFORE SPRING.

Sol's fingers closed on the oilskin pouch. The bond didn't crinkle. It had been pressed flat by days in her coat, the ink black and certain. The Marrow's surety. Her boat. All of it, offered for six highland berths before the storm bell sealed the channel for the season.

She knocked again. "Quill. I'm not leaving until you look at it."

A bell sounded somewhere below, deep and slow—the storm bell marking the pause before the lock teeth dropped. Through the glass, Sol saw movement inside. Not Quill. A shadow shifting behind the counter, then stillness.

The chain on the book gleamed in the lantern light. The count was full. Six names, or seven, or however many Quill had squeezed in before the tide turned. Sol's name wasn't among them. The Marrow wasn't either. She had come to trade a boat for a future, and the warden had shut the door.

She set her shoulder against the shutter. It didn't move. The padlock was new, the steel cold under her palm.

"Open it," Sol said, her voice low. "I know you're in there."

The lock teeth began to turn below her with a groan of metal on metal, the gate sealing itself against the rising water. She had minutes, maybe less, before the channel locked and no boat—hers or anyone else's—could pass until spring.

The chain through the shutter's hasp had a hand's width of slack in it. Sol hooked two fingers under the shutter and pulled until the links went tight, and the steel came up three inches and stopped.

Quill's eye filled the gap. Then the rest of her face, green-lit from the lantern behind her, wearing the look of a woman who had been awake for two tides and had decided to make that everybody's problem.

"Four words," Quill said. "I put four words on a slip for you and you came back with your shoulder."

"Read this instead." Sol flattened the oilskin on the sill and fed the bond through the gap. Wax, ribbon, the *Marrow* written out in a clerk's careful hand. "The hull against six highland berths. Surety means you take the boat if I default, cut her up for scrap, and the rest of the debt stays yours. That's a good trade and you know it."

"I know what surety is. I write them." Quill didn't touch the paper. "It's forfeit."

"It's sealed."

"Forfeit and sealed aren't opposites, captain." She said it the way another woman would read a depth off a line. "Your bond died at slack water on the ninth, when two children were standing on your deck where the Factor's twelve thousand should have been. Not void. *Forfeit.* The difference is the whole of it."

Below, the Marrow's engine note climbed and held. Sol could hear Dey swearing at the throttle in the flat, patient voice he used when he was frightened and wouldn't say so. She had that hour now, or the account of it — her own voice off a slate, calm, saying the children come up first. She could recite it start to finish. She could not remember standing inside it.

"Then price the hull," she said. "Scrap value. Now. Tonight."

"The hull isn't mine to price and you'd not like the number." Quill's chin came up. "You're not buying with a boat anyway. You're buying with a story about metal under the Line, and I've heard that one off every crew that's ever come up my stair wet."

"I'm not asking for credit. I'm asking you to write six names."

"Then write them yourself." Quill nodded at the chained book. "Pen's inside. So's the tide table, the count, and forty-one people who paid in coin, in medicine, in a son's indenture, in a hand. Nothing you set on this counter moves that number. Not wax, not paper, not brass."

Sol took the sounding lead off her belt — her mother's, worn smooth, a lump of gray metal on four fathoms of line — and laid it in the gap. Quill looked at it for exactly as long as it took to be sure.

"That's a good lead," she said. "It isn't a berth."

"Everyone has a price, warden."

"You've been talking to the Factor's people." Quill's mouth flattened. "I don't have prices. I have a book. Prices are for people who can bend a thing and still sleep."

"Forty-one," Sol said. "You've never been under forty meters in your life, and you'll stand there and tell me what my crew forgets down there like it's a matter of tidy handwriting."

"I've never been below the Line and I don't intend to be." Quill's voice didn't rise, which was worse. "Down there a man forgets his mother's face and blames the water. Up here we call that not writing things down."

Sol put both palms flat on the sill, in the three-inch gap, and left them there. The lock teeth turned another notch under her boots and the whole stair shuddered, and out on the black water the Marrow's horn gave one short blast — Dey, saying *hurry* in the only language he had left that the salt hadn't taken.

"Your ninety seconds are going," Quill said.

"Open the shutter."

"No." Quill reached down, and the shutter dropped back against the chain with a bang that Sol felt in her teeth. Through the glass she watched the warden uncap a pen, pull the chained book toward the lantern, find a line near the top of the page, and draw one clean stroke through the name of the boat.

Sol got her fingers into the gap before the hasp settled.

The chain bit across the backs of her fingers. She held the shutter up anyway, three inches of lantern light and cold air between her and the one woman on the coast who could not lie to her.

"Then don't take the hull," Sol said. "Take what's under it."

Inside the box, the pen stopped.

"Mercy General kept a mint annex," Sol said. "Coast mint coin came off the boats in sheets, still in the paper. Never spent, never in a pocket, nothing on it has a debt attached because it's never been anywhere. It's under the pharmacy at thirty-eight meters, behind the service trunk — that's the pipe-and-cable shaft that runs down a tower so you don't cut through floors. Two seals, dogging clamps, the kind you back off with a bar. Slack water. Hour down, hour up, box in the drum. You hold it against six names, and if I'm late you can be sick on the money."

"Mint gold." Quill said it the way she'd said *forfeit*.

"You've seen a strongbox."

"I've seen everything anybody's ever laid on that counter to move my count." The lantern behind her swung with the stair. "Two winters back a man off the *Corvid* stood exactly where you're standing with a vault under the Line, a chart, and a diver who'd seen it with his own eyes. I wrote down what he asked. He went for it in a flat sea. The boat came back with his line still on the drum and no man on the end of it."

"His boat. His line." Sol put more shoulder into the shutter. "I've got a boat, a crew, and a bell-tender who knows the Stair. You want the hull, you can have the hull. I want six names written before those teeth drop."

"My book doesn't take metal under the Line." Quill's voice didn't move at all, which was how Sol knew she'd lost this. "It takes bodies standing in berths right now. Breathing. With names I can read back to them and get an answer. Forty-one of them, and every one paid something I could put in a column — coin, medicine, a son's indenture, a hand. Metal under the Line isn't a berth. It's a story a man tells while he's still wet."

Sol turned her head. Down the gate's low stair, in the lee of the warden's box, Mara Vos sat on a step with her hands on her knees and a gray blanket over her shoulders, counting. Not fast. Even, patient, like a woman paying something out in small coins. Thirty-four. Thirty-five. Salas stood above her, hood up, a coil of line in his fists, not helping and not leaving, the way he'd stood for months.

"Who's she counting for?" Sol said.

"Started at one the hour she came up my stair and she hasn't stopped since. I asked her what she's counting. She said *seconds*." Quill's eyes went past Sol to the water. "I told her I've a bell-tender for that."

Out on the black channel the Marrow yawed as a swell came through the gate, and the engine note dropped and caught. "Bayo!" Sol bellowed. "Wheel! Dey, up here!"

Something answered from the bow, and Dey's boots came off the deck and onto the steel.

Thirty-six.

"I never wrote a lie in that book," Quill said. "Not one line, and I'm not starting tonight for a captain with a story."

Thirty-seven.

Mara stopped. Her head came up, and she looked at the underside of the warden's box, or through it.

"Thirty-eight," she said.

Then the count moved on, thirty-nine, forty, and Sol stood with her hands full of shutter, listening to the voice that had come out of a drowned slate that morning, sitting ten feet away on a wet step in a blanket, giving away seconds she didn't have.

"That's the count," Quill said. "Full means full."

Dey's boots hit the top rung, and under the counter Quill's hand went to a drawer and drew it open.

Dey's boots hit the top rung and he braced one hand on the warden's box, the other still wrapped in the salt-burn rag. The stair shuddered under him as the lock teeth turned another notch, a groan that went up through the soles. He smelled lantern oil, cold iron, and the wet wool of the blanket on the woman counting on the steps below.

"Thirty-nine," she said. "Forty."

Quill's hand came through the shutter gap, fingers pale in the lantern light, pushing a folded sheet of paper toward him. The ink was fresh enough to smear if he touched it wrong.

"Your indenture," Quill said. "Comes due at the next tide. That's three hours, maybe four before the channel locks. The order inked on it says you dive the debt off or you come off the *Marrow* into the Factor's keeping. Either way, you're not crew when the water rises."

Dey took the paper. Didn't unfold it. Just held it up to the lantern and read the block print upside down, his thumb finding the crease where it had been folded in thirds.

*Indentured Diver Dey Okafor. Debt: twelve thousand credits plus interest accrued. Due: high tide, storm bell pause. Satisfaction: one dive of warden's designation at or below the Line, or transfer of person to Factor Rusk's barge for the remainder of term.*

The Factor's barge was at the bottom of the channel now, Rusk with it. But the Factor had other collectors, other barges, and the debt didn't die with the man who held the note.

"Three hours," Dey said. He let the paper hang from two fingers. "You want me to dive the debt off in three hours, warden, I'm gonna need grease to fit down anything. These shoulders don't fold like they used to."

He grinned at the shutter gap, at Quill's eye, at Sol's knuckles white on the chain. The grin felt normal. The kind of normal he'd built out of salt and not-showing.

Then his chest seized.

It started behind the sternum, a hook catching, and he coughed once — hard, wet, the sound of something tearing loose inside. Then again. And again. His knees buckled and he caught the stair rail with his good hand, the rag slipping from the burned one, skin raw and pink against the cold steel.

The counting on the steps below didn't pause. *Forty-one. Forty-two.*

Salas didn't move. Just stood with his coil of line and his hood up, a statue in oilskins, watching Dey hack up his lungs on the Kettle's top step.

Dey's vision grayed at the edges. He'd done this before — the cough that came from breathing too deep too long, the scrubber canister spent at thirty meters and the pressure doing what pressure does to tissue that isn't meant for it. He'd thought the rest at the surface would clear it. He'd thought a lot of things.

"Forty-three," Mara said.

The coughing slowed. Left him hanging on the rail, spit and something darker on his lips, the indenture paper crumpling in his fist. He forced a breath. Then another. The hook in his chest settled into a dull ache.

"Grease," he said again, voice scraped thin. "And a line that doesn't snap. And maybe a warden who writes 'or' like she means it."

He looked up at the shutter gap, at Sol holding the chain, at Quill's face behind the glass. The storm bell was silent now — the pause over, the teeth turning steady and slow, the channel closing itself for the season.

"Three hours," he said. "I'll need a scrubber that works. And a boat that waits."

"Three hours," Quill said. "I heard him. The tide isn't mine to move either."

Dey opened his mouth. Sol got there first.

"Down, Dey. Take Bayo and count crates on the afterdeck. Out loud, both of you, so I know you're still breathing up here."

"I can count and cough at the same time," Dey said. "It's my one marketable skill." He got two rungs down, then stopped with his good hand on the rail. "If she writes an *or* beside my name, I want it read out where the crew can hear it."

"Nobody's writing your name tonight."

"That's what's got me worried." He went down.

Mara's voice came up through the steel, even as a bilge pump. *Forty-six. Forty-seven.* Salas shifted his grip on his coil of line and looked at nothing in particular.

Sol set her shoulder to the shutter and lifted until the chain drew tight across her knuckles.

"One name," she said. "Mine. Write me in and I'll stand whatever work the hill has open. Sluices, pumps, hauling. I'm not asking for a bunk with a window."

"You're asking for a bunk." Quill's eye went to Sol's hands and came back up. "A berth is a number, a bunk, and a draft of water under it, and there's nine people in my corridor who'd take your sluice work, sleep in a stairwell, and thank me for it."

"Then write me and I'll sleep in the stairwell."

"Forty-one," Quill said. "Paid, standing, and answerable by name. I don't have a column for a captain with a story."

"You've got a column for everything else on this coast."

"I've got a column for what's in front of me." Quill uncapped the pen and didn't use it. "You want the Line? First week I had this box I wrote on the flyleaf, in my own hand: *a man who comes up short has been robbed, do not write it against his name.* Forty meters down the hours start going and they don't come back. That's not untidiness and it's not drink. I've written that same line forty-one times tonight and I meant it every time. So I know the difference between a man who forgot his mother's face and a man who never learned it."

"Then you know more than the rest of us."

"I know enough to ask." The pen went flat on the counter. "The book takes a name I can read out at muster and get an answer to. That's the whole of my trade. I write a hollow name, I've taken a berth off somebody who can still answer, and I'll not do that to be kind to you. So. How many hours are you missing?"

The teeth turned under the stair. *Forty-eight.*

"I remember the ninth," Sol said. "Every minute of it. My own voice on the slate, calm as a clerk, saying the children come up first."

"A slate remembers for you. That's what it's for — a machine with a memory and no mouth." Quill leaned into the gap until the lantern lit the underside of her jaw. "I asked what *you're* missing."

Sol laid her hand flat on the sill, in the three inches of light, and pressed down until the tendons stood up in her wrist. The chain lay across her other hand and she let it lie there.

"Weather," she said. "Same storm four days running. Ask me which day I lost the wheel to a swell and which day I handed it over and I'll give you the same answer twice."

"That's a joke with the true thing folded inside it." Quill didn't blink. "I've had forty-one of those through this window tonight. Every soul on my stair gives me a number and every number is short, because nobody rounds up on themselves. Give me yours and I'll know what I'm writing."

*Forty-nine,* Mara said. *Fifty.*

Sol's hand stayed where it was, white at the fingertips where the ledge bit, the flat-palmed grip of a woman holding a thing shut with her own weight.

Below, the Marrow's horn went off twice, short, and Bayo's voice came up the stair calling her name in the tone he used for a line about to part.

Quill straightened out of the light. Sol heard the small dry sound of a key lifted off a nail.

"Stand where I can see your hands," Quill said. "I'll read it out myself, since you won't."
